title: Dating 101 (avoid these mistakes)
summary: Part 2 of the sisters' dating series for ambitious women: Jean shares a couples-therapy exercise for stack-ranking life priorities with a partner, they debate whether LinkedIn should be used for dating, and Jean recounts her egg-freezing journey while Cherie calls not freezing hers a big regret. Key takeaways: interrogate values early, use professional networks for background checks rather than cold advances, check employer fertility benefits, freeze eggs rather than embryos to protect yourself, and treat egg freezing as a test of whether a partner is truly 50/50.

ideas.idea: Stack-rank the five or six most important elements of life (career, health, family of origin, partner, future children, God) and compare lists with your partner to test value alignment.
ideas.detail: Jean learned this exercise in couples therapy with her ex-fiance and was shocked at the big differences that surfaced even after eight years together; the earlier you do it, the more clarity you have.

ideas.idea: Partners don't need identical rankings, but each must be comfortable and happy with the other's stack ranking.
ideas.detail: One person can rank children first and the other career first and it can work if they agree on the roles that implies, such as primary caretaker and breadwinner; at minimum the exercise forces the conversation.

ideas.idea: Being best friends who feel similar makes it easy to project alignment onto a partner and assume shared priorities that were never verified.
ideas.detail: Jean says two otherwise well-adapted, successful people never got to the bottom of their priorities in eight years because those topics don't come up naturally in conversation.

ideas.idea: Couples counseling, including premarital counseling before engagement, is healthy and should be done earlier and more consistently rather than as a last resort.
ideas.detail: Jean did double one-hour sessions every Sunday and was emotionally drained afterward; she wishes they had done it earlier, and notes a friend doing premarital counseling before even getting engaged, which is quietly becoming more common though still stigmatized.

ideas.idea: If you're not ready to do the values exercise with a partner, do it alone first: rank your own values, imagine theirs realistically, then work up to doing it together.
ideas.detail: The conversation can happen in five-minute chunks with breaks to think, rather than one big sitting; Jean cautions to keep the imagined version rooted in reality, 'no limerence.'

ideas.idea: Do not use LinkedIn to hit on people; unsolicited romantic InMails are inappropriate, harassing to women, and can get your profile reported and removed.
ideas.detail: Cherie, a former LinkedIn employee, says trust and safety teams actively fight this because LinkedIn profiles are public professional identities that cannot be made private.

ideas.idea: LinkedIn is useful for dating only as a background-check tool to verify someone is who they say they are and to see first-, second- and third-degree mutual connections.
ideas.detail: Cherie recommends running background checks for safety but says to take any outreach off-platform, e.g. via email.

ideas.idea: Treating dating like a full-time work stream with a funnel and quota is extreme but reflects the intentionality some ambitious women adopt after prioritizing career.
ideas.detail: Jean's friend paid a matchmaker $6,000 for three dates, joined clubs and all the apps, and teamed with a friend to cold-email LinkedIn prospects as each other's matchmakers; one man replied cc'ing his wife, and she ultimately met her fiance on Hinge and got engaged within seven months.

ideas.idea: As an entrepreneur without a school or office dating pool, treat everyone as a potential coworker and meet people through legitimate business introductions.
ideas.detail: Jean's serious relationships all started as friendships from school or work; a friend reframed her situation as 'now everyone is your coworker,' and Jean accidentally got a date from a business coffee introduced by a friend.

ideas.idea: Business school and top employers are pre-screened dating pools because admission and success there already verify ambition, accomplishment and how someone behaves with others.
ideas.detail: Cherie calls not making something work at Stanford GSB one of her biggest regrets; the sisters suggest looking one class year above or below your own, and Jean notes friends who married business school classmates 5-7 years after graduating.

ideas.idea: When evaluating a job offer, ask about egg-freezing and fertility benefits, which can cover a roughly $40,000 procedure.
ideas.detail: Big tech companies like LinkedIn, Microsoft, Meta and Snapchat cover it; a friend weighing a Snapchat offer against Meta specifically asked Jean about fertility benefits, and you may also be covered under a partner's plan.

ideas.idea: Not freezing eggs while at a corporate job with coverage is one of Cherie's biggest regrets, though the medical guidance five years ago discouraged it for women in their 20s and 30s expecting kids by their mid-30s.
ideas.detail: A 24-year-old Microsoft PM friend froze hers before Wharton, which impressed Cherie; Jean says OBGYNs and fertility doctors once discouraged it, but the sentiment has shifted toward preventive freezing, partly driven by fertility startups' marketing.

ideas.idea: Freeze eggs, not embryos, to protect yourself, since an ex-partner can block use of shared embryos.
ideas.detail: A friend of a friend froze embryos with her fiance after cancer, later divorced, and he refused to let her use them; Jean's doctor said freezing technology has improved so the success gap between frozen eggs and embryos is now only about 4%, so she chose eggs despite being about to get engaged.

ideas.idea: Egg freezing is grueling and like a mini pregnancy: self-injected hormones, patches, daily blood draws, mood and weight changes, and the burden falls entirely on the woman.
ideas.detail: Jean and her partner botched the first expensive dose while mixing it at home; she references Ronny Chieng's Netflix special about helping his wife inject hormones.

ideas.idea: Going through egg freezing together is a gauntlet that reveals what roles each partner naturally takes; a true 50/50 partner should handle all the appointments, prescriptions and paperwork while the woman bears the physical burden.
ideas.detail: Jean says the arrangement can differ as long as both agree, but if a man markets himself as a progressive 50/50 partner he must show it; Cherie calls it a better test than getting a dog together and part of dating 'information collecting.'

ideas.idea: Information from girlfriends is power; sharing personal experiences on fertility and dating empowers women to make life decisions with confidence, not just career ones.
ideas.detail: Jean explains she shares her egg-freezing and counseling story because she gained so much wisdom from friends and wants to pass it on.
